opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of it is that we're now building and deploying some of the most consequential technology in history, and we fundamentally don't understand how it works. These models are grown more than they're designed. We set up an architecture, we pour in an enormous amount of data and compute, and out comes this thing that can write code, reason about biology, hold a conversation. But if you ask, "Why did the model produce this particular output?" or "What concept is it actually using here?", for the most part we can't answer that. We treat them as black boxes.

And I think that's untenable long term, for a few reasons. One is safety and reliability. If you want to deploy these systems in high-stakes settings like healthcare, finance, or critical infrastructure, you need more than "it seemed to work on our evals." You want to know whether the model is relying on the right features or whether it's picked up some spurious shortcut that will break the moment the distribution shifts. Interpretability lets you look inside and check.

The second is control. Right now the main levers we have for shaping model behavior are things like prompting and fine-tuning, which are pretty blunt instruments. If you actually understand the internal representations, which neurons or features correspond to which concepts, you can intervene much more precisely. You can turn up or turn down specific behaviors and edit what the model knows. You can debug it the way you'd debug software, rather than just retraining and hoping for the best.

And the third, which I find really exciting, is discovery. These models have learned things from data that we humans may not know yet, especially models trained on scientific data like genomics or protein structures. If we can read out what they've learned, interpretability becomes a tool for scientific discovery itself, not just for auditing.

So at Goodfire, our view is that interpretability is a foundational capability that's needed to make AI systems safe, steerable, and genuinely useful, not just a nice-to-have research area. The analogy I like is that we're in a sort of pre-microscope era of AI. We're seeing all these powerful effects without being able to look at the underlying mechanisms. Our mission is to build those tools, so that understanding what's happening inside a neural network becomes as routine as reading a stack trace.

r001.rationale: It links interpretability to safety and reliability in high-stakes settings, explaining that inspecting internal features can reveal shortcuts that may fail when conditions change.

r002.rationale: It says models are grown more than designed and that understanding their representations enables precise interventions, but it does not clearly frame that access as enabling intentional model design.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that neural networks are the most important technology of our lifetime, and we fundamentally don't understand how they work. We train them, we observe their behavior from the outside, we poke at them with prompts, but the actual computation happening inside is essentially a black box. That's a strange position to be in with something this consequential.

At Goodfire, our view is that interpretability is the path to actually engineering these systems rather than just growing them and hoping for the best. Right now, if a model does something you don't want, your options are pretty blunt: you fine-tune, you add more data, you write a longer system prompt, and you check whether the behavior changed. You're treating the model like a biological organism you're trying to breed, not like a piece of software you can inspect and edit.

If you can read the internal representations, if you can see what features a model is using when it makes a decision, then you can intervene directly. You can find the circuit responsible for a behavior and steer it, remove it, or strengthen it. That's a qualitatively different relationship with the technology. It's the difference between a doctor who can only observe symptoms and one who has an MRI.

And I'd argue this matters more as the models get more capable, not less. The gap between what we can observe and what's actually happening inside is widening. So the mission is really about closing that gap, building the tools that let people understand, debug, and ultimately design neural networks with intention. If we're going to hand more and more decisions to these systems, we should be able to look inside them and know why they're doing what they're doing.

r001.rationale: The response says these systems are consequential and that we should understand their decisions, but it does not connect that understanding to reliable deployment in mission-critical contexts.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts engineering and intentionally designing models with merely growing them and hoping for the best.

astra-6.text:
Because if we want to build AI systems that we can reliably understand and steer, we need to see more than their inputs and outputs. Today, we largely train a neural network and then study its behavior from the outside. That tells us a lot, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us why it made a particular decision or how to change that behavior reliably.

At Goodfire, we see interpretability as a way to open up that black box—to understand what a model has learned and how it uses that knowledge. And the goal isn’t just to produce an explanation. It’s to make that understanding actionable, so we can diagnose failures, guide behavior, and build better systems.

That’s why understanding the internals is central to the mission. It gives us a path toward treating these models as systems we can deliberately engineer, with a clearer understanding of what we’re changing and why.

r001.rationale: The response says internal understanding can help build AI systems that are reliably understood and steered, but it does not mention deployment in mission-critical contexts.

r002.rationale: The response describes deliberately engineering models, but does not contrast that with merely growing models from data.

sol-6.1.text:
At Goodfire, we believe that if we want to build AI we can reliably steer, we need to understand what’s happening inside these models. Today, we mostly shape their behavior from the outside: we give them training examples, evaluate their outputs, and adjust things when they get something wrong. That’s powerful, but it leaves a lot hidden.

Interpretability gives us a path toward understanding the internal mechanisms behind that behavior. What has a model learned? Which concepts is it using? Why does it produce a particular response? If we can answer those questions, we can start making more precise interventions.

That’s central to our mission: turning neural networks into systems we can understand and intentionally shape. Understanding their inner workings is what connects explaining a model’s behavior to actually improving it.

r001.rationale: It connects understanding internal mechanisms to reliably steering AI, but does not mention deployment or mission-critical contexts.

r002.rationale: It says understanding internal mechanisms enables precise interventions and intentionally shaping models, contrasting this with shaping behavior only through training examples and outputs.
